title: 7. Redis & Caching
description: Turing FDE core: Redis data types, caching patterns (cache-aside, write-through, write-behind), pub/sub, Redis Streams, Cluster, Sentinel, cache invalidation, TTL strategy, and common pitfalls.

7.1 Redis Data Types: String: GET/SET/INCR/DECR/APPEND — counters, simple cache, rate limits
Hash: HSET/HGET/HMGET/HGETALL — user profiles, session objects
List: LPUSH/RPUSH/LPOP/LRANGE — queues, activity feeds, recent items
Set: SADD/SMEMBERS/SINTER/SUNION/SDIFF — unique tags, friend lists, deduplication
Sorted Set: ZADD/ZRANGE/ZRANGEBYSCORE/ZRANK — leaderboards, priority queues, rate limit sliding window
HyperLogLog: PFADD/PFCOUNT — cardinality estimation (unique visitors) with ~0.81% error, 12KB
Stream: XADD/XREAD/XGROUP — durable log with consumer groups (like Kafka, but simpler)
7.2 Caching Patterns: Cache-aside (lazy): app checks cache → miss → read DB → write cache. App owns cache population.
Write-through: write to cache AND DB synchronously on every write. No stale data; write latency doubles.
Write-behind (write-back): write to cache only; flush to DB async. Risk: data loss on crash.
Read-through: cache itself fetches from DB on miss — transparent to app. Used by managed caches (ElastiCache DAX).
Refresh-ahead: proactively refresh cache before TTL expires (for hot keys).
7.3 Pub/Sub & Streams: SUBSCRIBE/PUBLISH: fire-and-forget, no persistence, no consumer groups. Miss messages if offline.
Redis Streams (XADD): persistent, consumer groups, ACK, replay — use when Kafka is too heavy.
Use pub/sub for: real-time notifications, cache invalidation broadcast, live dashboards.
Use Streams for: reliable async job queues, event sourcing light, audit logs at small scale.
7.4 Redis Cluster & HA: Sentinel: monitors masters, promotes replica on failure — no horizontal scaling, single master writes.
Cluster: 16384 hash slots across N master nodes, each with replicas. Horizontal scaling.
Client must be cluster-aware (ioredis cluster mode). MGET/MSET only work on same-slot keys.
Hot key problem: one slot overloaded. Fix: key spreading (append random suffix, fan-out reads).
WAIT command: synchronous replication check before responding (stronger durability guarantee).
7.5 Cache Invalidation: TTL: simplest strategy — stale for up to TTL seconds.
Event-driven: on DB write, DEL or SET the cache key (requires app discipline).
CDC + pub/sub: Debezium watches DB WAL → publishes to Redis pub/sub → all app nodes invalidate.
Tag-based: group keys by tag (user:{id}:*), DEL by pattern (SCAN + DEL — never KEYS in prod).
Stampede protection: XFetch algorithm or mutex lock on cache miss.

questions.prompt: You need a leaderboard: store scores for 1M users and query top 100 by score efficiently. Which Redis type?

options.text: List
Hash
Sorted Set
Set

questions.explanation: Sorted Set (ZADD / ZRANGE ... WITHSCORES / ZREVRANGE) stores members with float scores, sorted automatically. ZREVRANGE 0 99 returns top 100 in O(log N + 100). Lists don't have scores. Hash doesn't sort.

questions.prompt: Best Redis command to implement an atomic counter (e.g. API hit count per user)?

options.text: SET counter GET + SET counter newVal
INCR counter
HSET counters user 1
LPUSH counter 1

questions.explanation: INCR is atomic — increment + return in one command. No race condition. Combine with EXPIRE for time-windowed counters. HSET works too (HINCRBY) but INCR is simpler for a single counter.

questions.prompt: You need to count unique visitors per day. You have 100M events/day and can tolerate ~1% error. Which structure saves the most memory?

options.text: Set — SADD all visitor IDs
Sorted Set with score=1
HyperLogLog — PFADD + PFCOUNT
Hash with visitor_id as field

questions.explanation: HyperLogLog uses ~12KB per key regardless of cardinality, with ~0.81% error. A Set would need ~1.6GB for 100M string IDs. Perfect for unique visitor counts, unique search terms, etc. where approximate is acceptable.

questions.prompt: You want to implement a FIFO job queue in Redis. Which commands?

options.text: LPUSH to enqueue, LPOP to dequeue
RPUSH to enqueue, LPOP to dequeue
ZADD to enqueue, ZPOPMIN to dequeue
SADD to enqueue, SPOP to dequeue

questions.explanation: RPUSH pushes to the right (tail); LPOP pops from the left (head) — FIFO. LPUSH+RPOP also works (mirror pattern). Use BLPOP for blocking pop (consumer waits for work). ZADD/ZPOPMIN is for priority queues.

questions.prompt: Which are good use cases for Redis Sets? (select all)

options.text: Tracking which users have seen an onboarding tooltip
Finding mutual friends between two users (SINTER)
Storing a user's profile fields
Deduplicating inbound webhook event IDs
Storing ordered purchase history

questions.explanation: Sets: unique unordered members, O(1) SISMEMBER, O(N) SINTER. Perfect for: seen-flags, social graph intersections, dedup. Hash is for profile fields (field-value pairs). List/SortedSet for ordered history.

questions.prompt: Implement a sliding window rate limiter (1000 req/min per user) using a Sorted Set. What score do you use?

options.text: Score = 0 for all entries
Score = current Unix timestamp in milliseconds
Score = incrementing counter
Score = user_id hash

questions.explanation: ZADD ratelimit:{user_id} <timestamp_ms> <request_id>. Then ZREMRANGEBYSCORE 0 (now-60000) to remove old entries. ZCARD gives requests in the last minute. Atomic Lua script wraps all three commands. Timestamp as score enables time-range queries.

questions.prompt: You SET a key with EXPIRE 60. Then you call SET again on the same key. What happens to the TTL?

options.text: TTL resets to 60 seconds
TTL continues counting down from where it was
The TTL is removed — the key now persists forever
Redis throws an error

questions.explanation: SET (without EX/PX option) replaces the key AND removes any existing TTL — the key becomes persistent. Use SET key value EX 60 or call EXPIRE again after SET if you want TTL preserved.

questions.prompt: What's the key difference between cache-aside and read-through caching?

options.text: Cache-aside stores compressed data; read-through stores raw data
Cache-aside: app manages cache population on miss. Read-through: cache layer fetches from DB on miss — transparent to app.
Read-through is only for write-heavy workloads
They are identical patterns with different names

questions.explanation: Cache-aside: app → check cache → miss → app queries DB → app writes to cache. App owns cache logic. Read-through: app → check cache → miss → cache fetches DB → returns to app. Simpler app code but less control. AWS ElastiCache DAX (DynamoDB) is read-through.

questions.prompt: When would you choose write-behind (write-back) over write-through caching?

options.text: When data consistency is critical and you can't afford any stale reads
When write throughput is high and you can tolerate potential data loss on cache crash
Write-behind is always safer than write-through
When the database is faster than the cache

questions.explanation: Write-through: write cache + DB synchronously → consistent but adds write latency. Write-behind: write cache only, flush to DB async → lower write latency, higher throughput, but data in cache not yet in DB can be lost on crash. Use for analytics counters, session updates where small loss is tolerable.

questions.prompt: You deploy a new service and the cache is cold. The DB gets hammered. How do you prevent this?

options.text: Increase DB connection pool before deploy
Pre-warm the cache: load hot keys from DB before routing traffic; use refresh-ahead on known hot data
Deploy with TTL=0 so keys never expire
Blue-green deploy always solves cold cache

questions.explanation: Cache warm-up strategies: (1) pre-populate hot keys during deploy before traffic hits; (2) shadow traffic to warm new cache; (3) blue-green: new env warms up while old serves traffic, cut-over once warm. TTL=0 is not a solution and blocks cache refreshes.

questions.prompt: An attacker sends requests for millions of non-existent IDs. Cache misses every time → DB hammered. What's this called and how do you fix it?

options.text: Cache stampede. Fix: distributed lock on miss.
Cache penetration. Fix: cache null results or use a Bloom filter to reject non-existent keys before hitting DB.
Cache avalanche. Fix: stagger TTLs.
Hot key problem. Fix: key spreading.

questions.explanation: Cache penetration: queries for keys that don't exist in cache or DB — cache never helps. Fix 1: cache null values (SET key NULL EX 60) so repeated queries for same non-existent ID hit cache. Fix 2: Bloom filter at the gate — if the filter says key doesn't exist, reject immediately without hitting DB.

questions.prompt: You cached 100k product pages all with TTL=3600. At midnight they all expire simultaneously. DB collapses. How do you prevent this?

options.text: Use a Bloom filter
Add jitter to TTL: TTL = base + random(0, spread) so expirations are spread over time
Use write-through instead of cache-aside
Increase Redis memory

questions.explanation: Cache avalanche: mass simultaneous expiration → thundering herd on DB. Fix: TTL jitter — TTL = 3600 + random(0, 600). Spreads expirations across 10 minutes instead of one instant. Also: circuit breaker on DB, mutex lock on hot key rebuild, or background refresh before expiry.

questions.prompt: Design a caching layer for a multi-tenant SaaS product listing API: 1M products, 50k req/sec read-heavy, data changes ~10 times/day per product. Handle invalidation, stampede, and per-tenant isolation.

rubric.criterion: Cache-aside with per-tenant key namespace: product:{tenant_id}:{product_id}
TTL with jitter (e.g. 3600 ± 300s) to prevent avalanche on mass expiry
Stampede protection: Redis SET NX mutex or XFetch probabilistic refresh
Event-driven invalidation on write: DEL/SET cache key when product updated
Cache null for missing products to prevent penetration attacks
Hot key handling: replicate top products across N keys with random suffix + fan-out read
Monitoring: hit rate per tenant, miss rate, memory usage, eviction rate

questions.modelAnswer: Key schema: product:{tenant_id}:{product_id} — tenant isolation by key prefix. Cache-aside: GET → miss → query DB → SET EX (3600 + rand(0,300)). On product update (write path): DEL product:{tid}:{pid} or SET with new value + TTL. Stampede: SET NX lock:{tid}:{pid} EX 5 before DB query; others wait BLPOP or return stale while lock holder rebuilds. Null caching: SET product:{tid}:{pid} '__NULL__' EX 60 for non-existent products. Hot key (e.g. featured product hit by all tenants): fan-out to product:{tid}:{pid}:r{0..9}, read random replica. Monitoring: cache hit rate (target >95%), Redis memory (set maxmemory + allkeys-lru eviction), eviction count alert. Per-tenant cache isolation also allows clearing all cache for one tenant: SCAN 0 MATCH product:{tid}:* UNLINK.

questions.prompt: Which data is generally GOOD to cache? (select all)

options.text: User profile data that changes rarely
Real-time stock prices (sub-second updates)
Computed aggregates (monthly report) that take 5s to generate
Session tokens
A user's bank account balance used in payment decisions

questions.explanation: Good cache candidates: rarely-changing data (profiles), expensive computations (reports), session tokens. Bad: real-time data (stock prices change too fast, stale = wrong trades), financial balances for payment decisions (must be authoritative — read from DB, not cache).

questions.prompt: A subscriber to a Redis pub/sub channel disconnects for 5 seconds and reconnects. What happens to messages published during the disconnect?

options.text: Messages are buffered and delivered on reconnect
Messages are permanently lost — Redis pub/sub has no persistence or replay
Messages are stored for 60 seconds by default
Redis retries delivery 3 times

questions.explanation: Redis pub/sub is fire-and-forget with no persistence. Subscribers that are offline miss messages permanently. For reliability, use Redis Streams (XADD/XREAD) which persist messages and support consumer groups with ACK.

questions.prompt: When should you choose Redis Streams over Redis pub/sub?

options.text: When you need real-time broadcasting to many subscribers
When you need durable messages, consumer groups, and replay from a specific offset
When you need the lowest possible latency
Streams are always better — pub/sub is deprecated

questions.explanation: Redis Streams: persistent log, consumer groups (XGROUP), ACK semantics, replay from any ID — a lightweight Kafka alternative. Use when message durability matters. Pub/sub: pure real-time fan-out with no durability — use for ephemeral signals (live dashboard updates, cache invalidation broadcast).

questions.prompt: You have 10 app servers each with local in-process caches of user data. A user updates their profile. How do you invalidate all 10 local caches?

options.text: Restart all 10 servers
Publish an invalidation event to a Redis pub/sub channel; all 10 servers subscribe and DEL the local cache entry
Use Redis keyspace notifications sent to a single server
Set a very short TTL on local caches

questions.explanation: Redis pub/sub is perfect for broadcasting cache invalidation signals across a fleet. Each server subscribes to invalidation:{service} channel. On write, publisher sends {userId}. All subscribers DEL their local copy instantly. Short TTL alone means stale for up to TTL seconds — pub/sub makes it near-instant.

questions.prompt: In Redis Streams, what does XACK do and why is it important?

options.text: Deletes the message from the stream permanently
Marks a message as processed by a consumer in its group — prevents redelivery to other consumers
Acknowledges to the publisher that a subscriber is connected
Commits the consumer's read offset like Kafka

questions.explanation: XACK marks a message as delivered and processed within a consumer group's Pending Entry List (PEL). Without XACK, the message stays in PEL and will be redelivered to another consumer on XCLAIM or after idle timeout. This is how Redis Streams provides at-least-once delivery.

questions.prompt: What's the key difference between Redis Sentinel and Redis Cluster?

options.text: Sentinel supports horizontal scaling; Cluster does not
Sentinel provides HA (automatic failover) for a single master; Cluster shards data across multiple masters for horizontal scaling + HA
They are identical — Sentinel is the older name for Cluster
Cluster is only for read replicas; Sentinel handles writes

questions.explanation: Sentinel: monitors one master + replicas, promotes a replica on master failure. No sharding — all data on one master, scales reads via replicas. Cluster: hash-slots across N masters, each master has replicas. True horizontal write scaling. Use Sentinel when data fits one node. Use Cluster when you need > one node worth of data or write throughput.

questions.prompt: Redis Cluster has 16384 hash slots. You add a 4th master node. What happens to the data?

options.text: All keys are rehashed and moved to the new node — brief downtime
A subset of slots is migrated from existing nodes to the new node — live, no downtime
The new node starts empty; existing data stays on old nodes
Cluster rebalances automatically with zero operator action required

questions.explanation: Redis Cluster uses MIGRATE to move slots from existing nodes to the new node live, one key at a time. During migration, both nodes serve reads/writes for the slot to avoid downtime. The reshard plan is computed and executed by the operator (redis-cli --cluster reshard). Not fully automatic — operator must trigger rebalance.

questions.prompt: In Redis Cluster, why does MGET user:1, user:2, user:3 fail with CROSSSLOT error?

options.text: MGET is not supported in Cluster mode
The keys hash to different slots (potentially different nodes) — multi-key commands require all keys in the same slot
The keys are too large for a single command
MGET requires a pipeline in Cluster mode

questions.explanation: Redis Cluster multi-key commands (MGET, MSET, SUNIONSTORE, etc.) require all keys in the same hash slot. Fix: hash tags — {user}:1, {user}:2 force keys with the same tag {} into the same slot. Or: pipeline individual GETs. Or: use a cluster-aware client that fans out.

questions.prompt: One Redis Cluster node is at 100% CPU while others are idle. What's the likely cause and fix?

options.text: Memory fragmentation. Fix: MEMORY PURGE.
Hot key — one key (or slot) receives disproportionate traffic. Fix: key spreading with random suffix + application-level fan-out reads.
Too many hash slots on that node. Fix: reshard.
Persistence (AOF) causing I/O bottleneck.

questions.explanation: Hot key problem: a single key (e.g. a globally popular product, feature flag) routes all traffic to one slot → one node. Fix: replicate the hot key across N slots (hot_key:r0 through hot_key:r9), write to all N, read from random(0,N-1). Or cache locally in app process for ultra-hot keys.

questions.prompt: Which Redis persistence options reduce data loss risk? (select all)

options.text: RDB (snapshotting) — full snapshot every N seconds/M writes
AOF (Append Only File) — logs every write command; fsync every second or always
AOF + rewrite to compact the log
WAIT N T — blocks until N replicas acknowledge the write
Disabling persistence entirely for max speed

questions.explanation: RDB: point-in-time snapshots, fast restart, can lose up to snapshot_interval of data. AOF every-second: max ~1s data loss. AOF always: max 1 write lost, ~2x write overhead. WAIT: synchronous replication confirmation. Disabling persistence = no durability guarantee.

questions.prompt: Redis maxmemory is reached. Which eviction policy should you choose for a general-purpose cache?

options.text: noeviction — return errors when full
allkeys-lru — evict least-recently-used key from all keys
volatile-lru — evict LRU keys only among those with TTL set
allkeys-random — evict a random key

questions.explanation: allkeys-lru: evicts the least-recently-used key from the entire keyspace — maximises cache effectiveness. volatile-lru only evicts TTL-bearing keys (safer if you mix persistent and cached data). noeviction is only for queues where losing data is unacceptable. Random eviction wastes hot keys.

questions.prompt: Which cache invalidation strategy gives the strongest consistency guarantee?

options.text: TTL-based — expire every 60 seconds
Write-through — update cache and DB in the same operation
Event-driven DEL on write — cache is invalidated exactly when the source changes
Refresh-ahead — pre-warm 10 seconds before TTL

questions.explanation: Event-driven invalidation (DEL on write) gives the tightest consistency — the cache entry is gone the moment the source changes. Write-through keeps cache consistent but adds write latency. TTL allows stale reads for up to TTL. Refresh-ahead still has a staleness window.

questions.prompt: In cache-aside, why is a simple DEL-on-write sometimes not enough? What is the double-delete (delayed double delete) pattern?

options.text: DEL is not atomic. Double delete ensures the key is deleted twice for reliability.

A concurrent reader can re-populate the cache with stale data between the DEL and the DB commit. Double delete: DEL before write + DEL again after a short delay (or after commit) to clean up any stale re-population.
Redis requires two DEL calls for cluster mode.
Double delete is for pub/sub scenarios only.

questions.explanation: Race: Thread A reads miss, fetches from DB (old value), Thread B writes new value + DELs cache, Thread A writes old value to cache. Cache is now stale again. Double-delete: DEL before write, commit to DB, then DEL again after short delay (or use a queue to schedule delayed invalidation). Eliminates the race window.

questions.prompt: You need to delete all cache keys matching product:{tenant_id}:*. Why should you use SCAN instead of KEYS?

options.text: KEYS is deprecated in Redis 6
KEYS blocks the entire Redis server until complete — O(N) scan of all keys. SCAN iterates incrementally without blocking.
SCAN is faster than KEYS for small keyspaces
KEYS doesn't support wildcards

questions.explanation: KEYS pattern is O(N) and blocks Redis (single-threaded) until complete — dangerous in production with millions of keys. SCAN uses cursor-based iteration returning small batches per call — non-blocking, safe for production. Use SCAN 0 MATCH product:{tid}:* COUNT 100 in a loop, then UNLINK (async DEL) on results.

questions.prompt: You have 10 microservices all caching user data. User profile changes in the users service. How do you invalidate caches in ALL other services reliably?

options.text: Each service polls the users table every 30 seconds
users service calls all 9 other services' cache-clear endpoints on every update
Debezium reads Postgres WAL → publishes user.updated event to Redis pub/sub or Kafka → all services subscribe and DEL their local cache entry
Set TTL=30s and accept stale data

questions.explanation: CDC (Change Data Capture) via Debezium captures every DB change from the WAL and publishes events. Decoupled: users service doesn't know who caches its data. All downstream services subscribe and react. More reliable than direct service calls (no synchronous coupling, resilient to downstream failures).

questions.prompt: A product catalog is cached in Redis. Prices update frequently (every few minutes) from a pricing engine. Occasional stale prices are acceptable for 30 seconds but not longer. Design the invalidation strategy.

rubric.criterion: TTL = 30s on all product cache keys — hard upper bound on staleness
Event-driven: pricing engine publishes price_updated event → DEL cache key immediately for fast invalidation
TTL jitter on initial set to prevent avalanche
Avoid KEYS pattern; use keyspace notifications or pub/sub for event propagation
For hot products: stale-while-revalidate — serve cached value, trigger async refresh, swap in new value when ready
Monitoring: cache hit rate, average staleness (emit timestamp in cached payload)

questions.modelAnswer: Set TTL=30 + random(0,5) on every SET — guarantees max 35s staleness even if event-driven invalidation fails. Pricing engine writes new price → publishes price_updated:{product_id} to Redis pub/sub channel → all app nodes subscribed DEL product:{id} immediately. On the next request, cache miss → fresh DB read → SET with TTL. For top 100 hot products (high read rate): stale-while-revalidate — serve cached value instantly, kick off async background refresh, swap value atomically with SET. Embed cached_at timestamp in payload — log staleness on each cache hit; alert if P99 staleness > 25s (approaching limit). Never use KEYS in prod — keyspace notifications or pub/sub for coordination.

questions.prompt: Why do you use a Lua script (EVAL) instead of a pipeline for rate limiting in Redis?

options.text: Lua scripts are faster than pipelines
Lua scripts execute atomically on the server — no other command runs between steps, eliminating TOCTOU races
Pipelines don't support INCR
Lua scripts bypass Redis memory limits

questions.explanation: Redis is single-threaded. A Lua script runs as a single atomic unit — no other client command can interleave. Pipelines batch network round trips but commands still run sequentially with possible interleaving from other clients. For check-then-act (rate limit: check count, increment, decide) you need atomicity → Lua or Redis Transactions (MULTI/EXEC).

questions.prompt: Why is Redis preferred over a relational DB for session storage?

options.text: Redis supports SQL queries on session data
O(1) GET/SET, built-in TTL for automatic expiry, sub-millisecond latency, horizontal scaling
Redis sessions are encrypted by default
Redis is cheaper than RDS

questions.explanation: Sessions are simple key-value reads/writes (session_id → serialized data). Redis: O(1), ~0.1ms, built-in TTL (EXPIRE) eliminates a cleanup job, easily distributed. RDBMS: needs an index on session_id, cleanup cron, slower under load, higher query overhead for a simple KV pattern.

questions.prompt: You configure a Redis replica and route reads to it. A write just landed on the master. What consistency guarantee do you have reading from the replica?

options.text: Strong consistency — replica is always up to date
Eventual consistency — replica replication is asynchronous; you may read stale data
Read-your-writes guarantee for the same connection
Replica reads are blocked until replication lag = 0

questions.explanation: Redis replication is asynchronous — master acknowledges writes before replicas apply them. Replicas may lag by milliseconds to seconds. No read-your-writes guarantee on replicas. Use WAIT command to force synchronous replication before returning, or always read from master when consistency matters.

questions.prompt: What does Redis MULTI/EXEC guarantee?

options.text: Full ACID transactions like a relational DB
Commands in the block are queued and executed atomically — no other client command runs between them — but errors don't rollback previous commands
Commands execute in parallel for speed
MULTI/EXEC provides optimistic locking automatically

questions.explanation: MULTI/EXEC: commands are queued until EXEC, then run atomically (no interleaving). However Redis transactions don't roll back on runtime errors — if INCR is called on a string, the error is returned but other commands in the block complete. Use WATCH for optimistic locking (abort EXEC if watched key changed).

questions.prompt: An enterprise client asks: 'We need Redis for session storage + real-time rate limiting across our 20-server fleet. It must survive a node failure with no downtime. What's your architecture?'

rubric.criterion: Redis Sentinel (for this scale) or Cluster — justify choice based on data size vs write throughput
Master + 2 replicas across 3 AZs for HA
Sentinel: 3 sentinel processes; automatic failover in seconds
Client-side: ioredis with Sentinel support / cluster mode + connection retry logic
Session: SETEX session:{id} 3600 {payload}; Cluster-mode clients handle slot routing
Rate limiting: Lua script (atomic INCR + EXPIRE); Redis single-thread guarantees no race
Monitoring: replication lag, memory usage, connected clients, eviction rate, hit rate

questions.modelAnswer: For session + rate limiting across 20 servers: assume data fits one node → Redis Sentinel. 1 master + 2 replicas in 3 AZs. 3 Sentinel processes (quorum=2) monitor master — failover in ~15-30s. App clients use ioredis sentinel mode: auto-discovers new master after failover, retries inflight commands. Sessions: SET session:{id} {payload} EX 3600 on every request update. Rate limiting: Lua script — INCR key; if result=1 EXPIRE key 60; if count > limit return 0 else return 1. AOF with fsync every second for durability. maxmemory-policy = volatile-lru (only evict session/rate-limit keys with TTL, never evict if no TTL set). ElastiCache Redis with Multi-AZ enabled is a managed alternative. Monitoring: CloudWatch (ReplicationLag, FreeableMemory, CacheHits, CacheMisses, Evictions) → alerts on lag > 50ms, memory > 80%, evictions > 0.

questions.prompt: Which scenarios are better served by a CDN cache than Redis? (select all)

options.text: Static assets (JS, CSS, images) served globally
User-specific API responses with authentication
Publicly cacheable API responses (product lists, blog posts)
Session tokens
Video and large media files

questions.explanation: CDN caches content at edge nodes globally, reducing latency and origin load. Perfect for: static assets, public API responses (Cache-Control: public), media. Not for: auth-required responses (per-user, cannot be shared), session tokens (private data).

questions.prompt: Why should you prefer UNLINK over DEL for deleting large keys in production?

options.text: UNLINK is atomic; DEL is not
DEL blocks the Redis main thread until the key memory is freed; UNLINK removes the key name synchronously but frees memory asynchronously in a background thread
UNLINK supports wildcards; DEL does not
UNLINK is faster for small keys

questions.explanation: DEL on a key with millions of members (a large Set or Hash) blocks Redis for the full deallocation time. UNLINK removes the key from the keyspace immediately (O(1)) and defers memory deallocation to a background thread — non-blocking. Always UNLINK large keys.

questions.prompt: What is stale-while-revalidate and when is it appropriate?

options.text: Return error if cache is stale; force fresh fetch
Serve the stale cached value immediately while triggering an async refresh in the background — balances freshness with low latency
Delete the cache entry and wait for a fresh value before responding
Return stale data permanently until the TTL expires

questions.explanation: Stale-while-revalidate: respond with the cached (possibly stale) value instantly (zero added latency for the user), kick off async refresh, update the cache when the fresh value arrives. Appropriate when: slight staleness is tolerable, low latency is critical, and refresh is cheap. Popularised by HTTP Cache-Control: stale-while-revalidate=N extension.

questions.prompt: You have 500 cache keys all related to tenant:42 (user lists, product lists, reports). How do you invalidate all of them when tenant:42 data changes?

options.text: FLUSHDB — clear all keys
KEYS tenant:42:* DEL — blocks Redis in production
Maintain a Redis Set (tenant:42:cache_keys) of all keys; SMEMBERS + UNLINK each member on invalidation
Set TTL=1 for all keys on invalidation

questions.explanation: Tag-based invalidation: when setting a cache key, also SADD tenant:42:cache_keys {key}. On invalidation: SMEMBERS tenant:42:cache_keys → UNLINK all members → DEL the tag set itself. This is O(N) but explicit and safe — no KEYS pattern, no FLUSHDB. Alternatively SCAN with MATCH in batches if you have a naming convention.

questions.prompt: What are Redis keyspace notifications and a practical use case?

options.text: Notifications sent when a key's memory exceeds a threshold
Pub/sub messages Redis publishes when key events occur (SET, DEL, EXPIRE, expired) — useful for reacting to TTL expiry without polling
Webhooks that Redis sends to registered HTTP endpoints
Log entries written when keys are accessed

questions.explanation: Enable with notify-keyspace-events Ex (expired events). Subscribe to __keyevent@0__:expired to receive a message when any key expires. Use case: session timeout reaction (clean up related data), delayed job execution (SET job:123 '' EX 60 → get notified in 60s to trigger the job).
